RagShortTexts: Shapur II negotiates power through aristocratic, military and religious relationships.
Armenian loyalties and campaign supplies affect Sasanian internal politics.

Variants.Content: Shapur II's Sasanian monarchy combines royal power with great aristocratic houses, military leaders and religious authorities. Influence comes through access to the king, land, service and regional connections, rather than a Roman senate under a different name. The frontier with Rome and struggles over Armenia make local loyalties especially important: a useful intermediary may also have reasons to change sides. Supplies for campaigns impose costs on estates and cultivators. In 374 internal politics therefore concerns how the king secures service and manages powerful supporters, not an inevitable sequence of poisonings or a uniform western European system of vassalage.

A rider called for service needs a fit mount and the provisions to reach the muster. An order issued at court still depends on local officers arranging transport and supply. If rival patrons dispute responsibility, men wait while their animals consume fodder; prestige at an audience does not feed a horse on the road.

An aristocratic supporter of Shapur weighs royal favour against regional ties and the obligations of military service. Armenia may offer influence while exposing an ally to pressure from both empires. Keeping a useful following requires resources, so a demand that exhausts an estate can weaken the very service the king expects from it.
